title: Christianity spreads beyond Judea
summary: After Jesus was crucified in Jerusalem, around 33 CE, his followers formed communities that spread quickly to Damascus and Antioch, where, according to the Book of Acts, they were first called Christians. From the mid-40s to the mid-50s CE the apostle Paul travelled through Cyprus, Asia Minor and Greece, founding churches among non-Jews, before dying in Rome around 64–65 CE, about the time Nero blamed the city's Christians for the Great Fire of 64.
why: Opening the movement to non-Jews turned a small Jewish sect into a religion that could travel along the Roman Empire's roads and sea lanes, and from there around the world.

title: Buddhism reaches China
summary: Buddhism reached China along the Silk Road in the 1st century CE. Tradition says Emperor Ming of the Eastern Han dreamed of a golden figure, sent envoys west and in 68 CE founded the White Horse Temple at Luoyang for two Indian monks, though many scholars treat the story as a pious legend. Firmer evidence comes in the 2nd century, when Central Asian monks such as the Parthian An Shigao (from 148 CE) and the Kushan Lokakṣema began translating Buddhist texts into Chinese at Luoyang.
why: The translation work begun at Luoyang carried Indian religious and philosophical ideas into the Chinese language, starting a transmission that made Buddhism a lasting part of Chinese life.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Silk Road transmission of Buddhism

title: Teotihuacan, metropolis of Mesoamerica
summary: Teotihuacan grew explosively in the first centuries CE into the largest city in Mesoamerica, laid out along the Avenue of the Dead with the Pyramid of the Sun, about 65 m high, completed by around 100 CE. At its height around 450 CE it may have housed about 100,000 people, though estimates range from 25,000 to well over that. Its ruling-class buildings were burned around 550 CE and the city declined; the Aztecs, who revered its ruins centuries later, gave it the Nahuatl name by which we know it.
why: Teotihuacan's power reached far beyond central Mexico: in 378 CE a warlord linked to the city took over the Maya city of Tikal and installed a new king, showing how one metropolis could shape politics across Mesoamerica.

title: Cai Lun improves papermaking
summary: In 105 CE Cai Lun, an official at the Eastern Han court, presented Emperor He with an improved way of making paper from tree bark, hemp waste, old rags and fishing nets. Paper already existed in China (the oldest surviving fragment, from Fangmatan in Gansu, dates to about 179–141 BCE), so historians see his work as improving and standardising an existing craft rather than inventing it, but his improvements led to paper's widespread use.
why: Cheaper and lighter than silk or heavy bamboo strips, paper gradually replaced them, letting whole books circulate and be carried by hand; Cai Lun came to be honoured as the traditional inventor of paper.

title: The Pax Romana and Rome at its height
summary: The Pax Romana, the roughly two centuries from Augustus (27 BCE) to the death of Marcus Aurelius (180 CE), was a time of relative peace and prosperity inside the Roman Empire, though not free of revolts and frontier wars. Under Trajan, who conquered Dacia and briefly annexed Armenia and Mesopotamia, the empire reached its greatest extent at his death in 117 CE. Its population is estimated to have peaked at about 70 million.
why: Long internal peace let trade flourish across the Mediterranean and beyond, and because it overlapped with Han China's own era of stability it stimulated travel and commerce right across Eurasia.

title: Kanishka and the Kushan crossroads
summary: The Kushan Empire, which ruled from Central Asia to northern India between about 30 and 375 CE, reached its peak under Kanishka, who reigned from about 127 to 150 CE from Purushapura (Peshawar) and Mathura. It linked Silk Road caravan routes with Indian Ocean sea trade, and Kanishka, though not himself a convert, patronised Buddhism and both the Gandhara and Mathura schools of Buddhist art.
why: Kushan control of the routes between India, Iran and China helped carry Buddhism, especially Mahayana Buddhism, into Central Asia and China.

title: Constantine, Christianity and a new Rome
summary: After defeating his rival Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge near Rome in 312, Constantine began favouring Christianity, and in 313 he and his co-emperor Licinius agreed at Milan to grant religious freedom and return confiscated church property. In 325 he summoned the Council of Nicaea, which produced the Nicene Creed, and on 11 May 330 he consecrated a new capital, Constantinople, on the site of Byzantium.
why: A persecuted faith became the emperor's favoured religion, and in 380 Theodosius I made it the empire's official one; Constantinople remained a Christian imperial capital until 1453.

title: The Gupta age in India
summary: From Pataliputra, Chandragupta I (crowned c. 320), his son Samudragupta and grandson Chandragupta II built an empire across northern India. The period is often called India's golden age, a label some historians dispute; the poet Kalidasa, the astronomer Aryabhata and the visiting Chinese monk Faxian, who praised its mild government, all belong to it. Hun invasions from the late 490s and rising regional rulers broke the empire up by the mid-6th century.
why: Gupta-era scholars produced lasting works of Sanskrit literature and science: Aryabhata, writing around 500, used place-value notation and gave π as about 3.1416, part of the tradition that produced modern numerals.

title: Aksum becomes a Christian kingdom
summary: Aksum, in today's northern Ethiopia and Eritrea, grew rich on Red Sea trade through its port of Adulis, exporting ivory, gold and tortoiseshell and minting its own coins; in the 3rd century the prophet Mani counted it among the world's four great powers with Rome, Persia and China. King Ezana, taught by Frumentius, a Christian from the Roman east, became its first Christian ruler, around 325–330 by most estimates, and his coins replaced the pagan disc and crescent with the cross.
why: Aksum became one of the earliest states anywhere to adopt Christianity, and Ezana made its Ge'ez script and language official alongside Greek, rooting a Christian, literate tradition in the Horn of Africa.

title: The Western Roman Empire falls
summary: On 4 September 476 the Germanic general Odoacer took Ravenna, deposed the young emperor Romulus Augustulus and sent the imperial regalia to the Eastern emperor Zeno in Constantinople instead of naming a new Western emperor. It capped a long decline that included mass migrations from 376, the sack of Rome in 410, civil wars and financial strain; historians also point to epidemics and climate change, and some prefer other end dates such as 480.
why: Western Europe passed to Germanic kingdoms while the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire carried on for nearly a thousand years more; 476 is often used to mark the end of antiquity.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Fall of the Western Roman Empire

title: Justinian's law code and reconquests
summary: The Eastern Roman emperor Justinian I (r. 527–565) had a commission led by Tribonian gather centuries of Roman law into the Code (529, revised 534), the Digest and the Institutes (533), later called the Corpus Juris Civilis. After the Nika riots of 532 burned the old church, he rebuilt Hagia Sophia, completed in 537, and his generals retook North Africa from the Vandals (533–534), Italy from the Ostrogoths (535–554) and part of southern Spain. From 541 plague, caused by the same bacterium as the later Black Death, swept the Mediterranean.
why: Recovered in Italy around 1070 and taught at Bologna, Justinian's law books became the foundation of the civil-law systems used across continental Europe and far beyond.

title: The Tang dynasty
summary: The Tang dynasty, founded in 618 after the collapse of the Sui, ruled China for nearly three centuries from Chang'an, a walled grid city of about 78 km² whose population inside the walls is estimated at 800,000 to 1 million. Merchants, monks and envoys from Central Asia, Persia, India and Arabia filled its markets, and the era is counted the greatest age of Chinese poetry, the age of Li Bai and Du Fu. The An Lushan rebellion (755–763) badly weakened the dynasty, which ended in 907.
why: Tang China was one of the most cosmopolitan societies of its time, and Chang'an's grid plan was copied for Japan's capitals at Nara and Kyoto and for Silla Korea's capital at Gyeongju.

title: Muhammad's Hijra to Medina
summary: Muhammad, born in Mecca around 570, began around 610 to report revelations that Muslims believe were delivered by the angel Gabriel and that form the Quran. Facing hostility from Mecca's ruling Quraysh, in 622 he and his followers migrated to Medina, then called Yathrib, where he became the community's leader and judge. Mecca surrendered to him in 629–630, and by his death in 632 most of the Arabian Peninsula had converted to Islam.
why: The Hijra marks the founding of the first Muslim community, and the caliph Umar later made it year one of the Islamic calendar, which Muslims still use.

title: Zero becomes a number
summary: Indian mathematicians had been writing numbers with base-10 place value for centuries (the earliest leaves of the Bakhshali manuscript are dated to about 224–383 CE), and around 500 Aryabhata marked empty places with the word kha, 'emptiness'. In 628 Brahmagupta, a native of Bhillamala, completed his Brahmasphutasiddhanta, the earliest known text to treat zero as a number in its own right, with rules for adding, subtracting and multiplying with zero and negative numbers.
why: Translated into Arabic at the Abbasid court, spread by al-Khwarizmi's book on Hindu numerals (c. 825) and brought into Europe from the 12th century, Indian place-value numerals with zero became the digits the whole world uses today.

title: The Arab Muslim conquests
summary: Within a few years of Muhammad's death, Arab Muslim armies defeated the Byzantines at Yarmuk and the Sasanian Persians at al-Qadisiyya (both 636), taking Syria, Iraq, Jerusalem (638) and Egypt (639–642); Persian resistance was broken at Nahavand in 642 and the last shah was killed in 651. Under the Umayyad caliphs, ruling from Damascus from 661, the conquests reached Spain and Sindh in 711, until the Franks defeated a raid near Tours in 732.
why: By 750 Muslim rulers governed, by various estimates, 11–15 million km² from Iberia to the Indus, and Arabic, made the language of government under the Umayyads, became a shared language of religion, law and learning across this vast area.

title: Vikings raid Lindisfarne
summary: In 793 Norse raiders plundered the island monastery of Lindisfarne, killing or enslaving many monks; the scholar Alcuin wrote that such terror had never before appeared in Britain. Over the next two and a half centuries Scandinavians raided, traded and settled from Ireland to the Russian rivers, where Rurik's successors founded Kievan Rus', served the Byzantine emperors, received Normandy in 911 and settled Iceland and Greenland. The age is traditionally closed by Harald Hardrada's death at Stamford Bridge in 1066.
why: Viking raiding, trading and settlement reshaped early medieval Europe, founding new states and linking the North Atlantic and the Baltic to Constantinople.
also: Around 1021 Norse Greenlanders were at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, a date fixed by tree rings; excavated by Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad from 1961, it is the only confirmed Norse site in North America outside Greenland, almost five centuries before Columbus.

title: Charlemagne crowned emperor
summary: Charlemagne, king of the Franks from 768 and of the Lombards from 774, conquered Saxony, Bavaria, northern Italy and part of northern Spain, uniting most of Western and Central Europe. On Christmas Day 800 Pope Leo III crowned him emperor in Rome. From his palace at Aachen he sponsored a revival of learning, the Carolingian Renaissance, led by scholars such as Alcuin of York, whose scribes spread the clear Carolingian minuscule handwriting.
why: Carolingian copyists made the earliest surviving copies of many Latin classics, including Cicero, Horace and Lucretius, and Charlemagne's lasting influence on the continent has earned him the title 'Father of Europe'.

title: The Classic Maya collapse
summary: In the 8th and 9th centuries the great Maya city-states of the southern lowlands broke down: dated monuments fell from about 40 a year around 750 to none by 900, and monumental building in the central area stopped after 830. Tikal, which may once have held tens of thousands of people, raised its last monument in 869 and was largely deserted by the end of the 10th century. Drought is now the leading explanation among more than 80 theories, alongside warfare, environmental damage and the collapse of trade routes.
why: The collapse shows how large, sophisticated societies can unravel, yet Maya civilization continued in northern Yucatán at cities such as Chichén Itzá and Mayapán, and independent Maya rule lasted until 1697.

title: Baghdad's House of Wisdom
summary: After the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur founded Baghdad in 762, the city became a centre of learning, and under al-Ma'mun (r. 813–833) a royal library known as the House of Wisdom became a hub for scholars translating Greek, Persian, Syriac and Indian works into Arabic. Hunayn ibn Ishaq translated Galen and Hippocrates, and al-Khwarizmi, who worked there around 820, wrote the book on al-jabr that gave us the word 'algebra'. Some historians doubt it was a formal academy, seeing the name as covering a library and Baghdad's wider community of scholars.
why: The translation movement preserved and built on ancient science and philosophy, and Arabic works such as al-Khwarizmi's later reached Europe in Latin; his Latinised name gave us the word 'algorithm'.

title: The Diamond Sutra, oldest dated printed book
summary: In Tang China printers carved whole pages into wooden blocks, inked them and pressed them onto paper. A printed scroll of the Buddhist Diamond Sutra, dated 11 May 868 and made 'for universal free distribution', was sealed in a cave library at Dunhuang, found there in 1900 and acquired by Aurel Stein in 1907; it is now in the British Library. It is the oldest surviving printed book that carries a date, though earlier undated prints exist.
why: Printing let texts be copied quickly and cheaply, and in the 1040s Bi Sheng took the next step in China with movable type made of baked clay, one character per piece.

title: Polynesians settle the remote Pacific
summary: Sailing double-hulled canoes and steering by the rising and setting points of stars and by ocean swells, Polynesian voyagers spread across thousands of kilometres of open Pacific. High-precision radiocarbon dating suggests the Society Islands were settled around 1025–1120 CE and that, in one rapid pulse around 1190–1290, voyagers reached the remaining islands of East Polynesia, including Hawaii, Rapa Nui (Easter Island) and Aotearoa New Zealand.
why: Without instruments or charts, Polynesian navigators settled the last large habitable islands on the map of the Pacific, spreading related languages and cultures from Hawaii to New Zealand and Rapa Nui.
also: Sweet potatoes, native to South America, were growing in the Cook Islands by about 1000 CE, which many researchers take as a sign that Polynesian voyagers reached the Americas and came back, though natural drift has also been proposed.

sources.title: Wilmshurst et al. 2011, PNAS: High-precision radiocarbon dating of East Polynesian colonization

title: Song China: gunpowder, compass and paper money
summary: Under the Song dynasty (960–1279), whose northern capital was Kaifeng, China's population roughly doubled and its economy boomed. In 1023–1024 the government took over the jiaozi notes first issued by Sichuan merchants, usually regarded as the first government paper money; the military manual Wujing Zongyao (compiled c. 1040–1044) holds the earliest known written formulas for gunpowder; and by 1088 Shen Kuo described the magnetic compass in use for navigation.
why: Gunpowder weapons and the compass, first recorded in Europe around 1190, later transformed warfare and sea travel worldwide, while state-backed paper money pointed the way to modern currency.

title: Cahokia, city of the Mississippians
summary: Around 1050 a sudden building boom beside the Mississippi, across the river from today's St. Louis, created Cahokia, the dominant centre of the maize-farming Mississippian culture. At its peak around 1100 it held perhaps 10,000–20,000 people, and its Monks Mound, about 30 m high and 290 m long, is the largest earthen mound north of Mexico. The city declined over the following centuries and was abandoned by about 1350.
why: Cahokia was the largest and most complex settlement north of the great cities of Mexico, showing that North America had its own urban societies long before Europeans arrived.

title: The East–West Schism
summary: On 16 July 1054 papal legates led by Cardinal Humbert laid a document excommunicating Patriarch Michael Cerularius on the altar of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople; days later the patriarch's synod excommunicated the legates in return. The quarrel capped centuries of disputes over the pope's authority, the filioque wording of the Nicene Creed and whether the Eucharist should use leavened or unleavened bread.
why: The break, hardened when crusaders sacked Constantinople in 1204, divided Christianity into a Roman Catholic West and an Eastern Orthodox East; the mutual excommunications were lifted only in 1965.

title: The First Crusade takes Jerusalem
summary: Answering a Byzantine appeal for help against the Seljuk Turks, Pope Urban II called at Clermont in November 1095 for an armed pilgrimage to Jerusalem. Crusaders set out in 1096, some bands massacring Jewish communities in the Rhineland on the way, took Antioch in 1098 and stormed Jerusalem on 15 July 1099, killing much of its population. They founded four crusader states: the Kingdom of Jerusalem, the County of Edessa, the Principality of Antioch and the County of Tripoli.
why: The crusade opened two centuries of holy war between Latin Christians and Muslim rulers in the Levant, and the crusading idea was later turned on Muslim Spain, the pagan Baltic and even Christian Constantinople.

title: Angkor Wat and the Khmer Empire
summary: The Khmer kings who ruled from Angkor from 802 built a vast 'hydraulic city' of reservoirs and canals; a 2007 survey found it was the largest pre-industrial city by area, with infrastructure spread over at least 1,000 km². King Suryavarman II (r. 1113–c. 1150) built Angkor Wat, a temple to Vishnu that is the largest religious complex in the world, and from 1181 Jayavarman VII added the walled city of Angkor Thom and made Mahayana Buddhism the state religion.
why: Angkor shows the scale a tropical rice-farming civilization could reach; it remained the Khmer capital until Ayutthaya sacked it in 1431 and much of its population moved south.

title: Genghis Khan unites the Mongols
place: Source of the Onon River, Khentii (Mongolia)
summary: In 1206 an assembly (kurultai) at the source of the Onon River proclaimed the Mongol chief Temüjin Genghis Khan, ruler of the united steppe peoples. He went on to force the Western Xia to submit, captured the Jin capital Zhongdu (modern Beijing) in 1215 and destroyed the Khwarazmian Empire in Central Asia from 1219, dying on campaign in 1227.
why: His heirs built the largest contiguous land empire in history, about 23.5 million km² by 1294, whose 'Pax Mongolica' carried goods, technologies and ideas across Eurasia.

title: Magna Carta
summary: Facing a rebellion by his barons, King John set his seal to a charter of liberties in the meadow at Runnymede, between Windsor and Staines, on 15 June 1215. It declared the English Church free and set limits on the king's demands, but Pope Innocent III declared it void within weeks and civil war followed. It was reissued in 1216, 1217 and 1225, and three of its clauses remain law in England and Wales.
why: Magna Carta came to stand for the principle that even the king is bound by law: later jurists and the American colonists invoked it, though it began as a settlement between the crown and the barons.

title: Great Zimbabwe
summary: Ancestors of today's Shona people began building in stone at Great Zimbabwe in the 11th century, and in the 13th and 14th centuries raised the Great Enclosure, whose mortarless walls stand up to 11 m high. The city was the capital of a kingdom that controlled the flow of gold from the Zimbabwean plateau to Swahili ports such as Sofala, and Chinese porcelain and glass beads found there show its links to Indian Ocean trade. Decline set in from the 15th century as power shifted to the Mutapa and Butua kingdoms.
why: Colonial-era writers credited the ruins to Phoenicians or the Queen of Sheba and Rhodesian authorities pressured archaeologists to deny African builders; only in the 1950s did its African origin become the scholarly consensus, making it a lasting symbol of pre-colonial African achievement.

title: The Mongols sack Baghdad
summary: In late January 1258 a Mongol army under Hulagu, a grandson of Genghis Khan, besieged Baghdad; the caliph al-Musta'sim surrendered on 10 February, the city was sacked and the caliph was put to death. Later writers claimed 800,000 or more dead, figures historians regard as inflated, though the true toll is unknown.
why: The sack ended the Abbasid caliphate in Baghdad after about 500 years and is traditionally seen as closing the Islamic Golden Age, although historians now see Baghdad's decline as more gradual and note that its libraries partly recovered within a few years.

title: The fall of Acre ends the crusader states
summary: In 1187 Saladin destroyed the crusader armies at Hattin and Jerusalem was lost, and later crusades, including the Fourth Crusade that sacked Christian Constantinople in 1204, failed to restore the crusader states. On 18 May 1291, after a six-week siege, the Mamluk sultan al-Ashraf Khalil captured Acre, the crusaders' last major stronghold, and their remaining mainland strongholds were lost the same year.
why: Acre's fall ended two centuries of crusader rule on the Levantine mainland; the crusades had deepened the split between Catholic and Orthodox Christians and helped Italian merchants come to dominate Mediterranean trade.

title: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage
summary: Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire (c. 1312–1337), crossed the Sahara on pilgrimage to Mecca, reaching Cairo in July 1324 with a vast retinue; later Arabic accounts tell of thousands of attendants and camels laden with gold, numbers historians treat as rhetorical rather than measured. The Cairo official al-Umari reported that Musa's spending lowered the value of gold there for at least twelve years. On his return Musa commissioned the Djinguereber Mosque in Timbuktu, around 1327.
why: Mali supplied almost half the Old World's gold in the early 14th century, and Musa's journey made West Africa's wealth famous in the Islamic world and Europe, where the Catalan Atlas of 1375 depicts him.

title: Tenochtitlan is founded
summary: According to their tradition, the Mexica settled where they saw an eagle with a snake in its beak perched on a cactus, on a swampy island in Lake Texcoco, traditionally in 1325. They enlarged the island with chinampa farm plots and joined it to the mainland with causeways, and after defeating Azcapotzalco in 1428 Tenochtitlan allied with Texcoco and Tlacopan in the Triple Alliance. By 1519 the city had over 200,000 people, and the empire it dominated covered most of central Mexico.
why: Tenochtitlan was the heart of the Aztec Empire until Spanish and Tlaxcalan forces besieged and destroyed it in 1521, and today's Mexico City stands on its ruins.

title: The Black Death
summary: Plague caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, probably originating in Central Asia, reached the Black Sea in the mid-1340s, when the Golden Horde was besieging the Genoese port of Caffa in Crimea; the famous story of plague corpses catapulted over its walls comes from a single, doubtful source. Genoese ships carried the disease to Constantinople and, in October 1347, to Sicily, and by 1353 it had swept Europe, the Middle East and North Africa, killing an estimated 25–60 percent of Europe's people and more than a third of Cairo's.
why: One of the deadliest pandemics in history, it left labour so scarce that wages rose in many places, while frightened communities turned on scapegoats: by 1351 some 210 Jewish communities had been destroyed.

title: Zheng He's treasure voyages
summary: Between 1405 and 1433 the Ming court eunuch Zheng He led seven great voyages into the Indian Ocean for the Yongle and Xuande emperors; the first had 317 ships and almost 28,000 men. Built largely at the Longjiang shipyard in Nanjing, the fleets called at Champa, Java, Malacca, Ceylon and Calicut, and later voyages reached Hormuz, Aden, Mogadishu and Malindi, returning with foreign envoys and gifts such as a giraffe.
why: The voyages displayed Ming power and drew distant states into China's tributary system, but the court abandoned them after 1433 amid high costs and Mongol threats in the north, decades before Portuguese ships entered the Indian Ocean.

title: Pachacuti builds the Inca Empire
summary: In the standard chronology, the Inca ruler Pachacuti came to power in 1438 after the Chanka attack on Cusco and began turning his small kingdom into an empire, Tawantinsuyu. He rebuilt Cusco as an imperial capital and probably built Machu Picchu as a royal estate, and his son Topa Inca pushed conquests north into Ecuador. By the early 1500s the empire stretched along the Andes from Colombia to Chile, tied together by the Qhapaq Ñan road network and run with quipu knotted-cord records.
why: It became the largest empire of the pre-Columbian Americas, governing perhaps 6–14 million people, before the Spanish conquest that began in 1532.

title: Gutenberg's printing press
summary: Around 1440 the German goldsmith Johannes Gutenberg developed a printing system that combined movable metal type cast in a hand mould, an oil-based ink and an adapted screw press. His Mainz workshop finished the 42-line Bible in 1454 or 1455, in an edition of perhaps 160–185 copies. Printing spread fast: by 1500 about 270 European cities had presses, which had turned out more than 20 million copies.
why: Cheap printed books spread literacy, scholarship and new ideas across Europe and helped make the Protestant Reformation possible, when Martin Luther became Europe's most published author.
also: Metal movable type had already been used in Korea, where the Jikji of 1377 is the oldest surviving book printed with it.

title: The fall of Constantinople
summary: On 6 April 1453 the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II laid siege to Constantinople with perhaps 50,000–80,000 troops and about 70 cannon, including a giant bombard cast by the engineer Orban, against some 7,000–8,000 defenders. After 53 days his forces broke through the 5th-century Theodosian Walls on 29 May; the last emperor, Constantine XI, died in the fighting, and Mehmed made the city his new capital.
why: The conquest ended the Byzantine Empire, the last remnant of the Roman Empire after nearly 1,500 years, showed that gunpowder artillery could breach the strongest walls, and is often taken to mark the end of the Middle Ages.

title: Columbus crosses the Atlantic
summary: Sponsored by Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain, Christopher Columbus sailed from Palos on 3 August 1492 with the Santa María, Pinta and Niña, hoping to reach Asia by sailing west. On 12 October he landed on an island its people called Guanahani, probably today's San Salvador in the Bahamas, then explored Cuba and Hispaniola. He made four voyages in all (1492–1504) and maintained that he had reached the Indies.
why: His voyages began lasting contact between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia: the Columbian exchange of crops, animals and diseases, and European conquest and colonization, as Old World diseases contributed to an estimated 80–95 percent fall in Native American populations within 100–150 years.

title: Vasco da Gama reaches India by sea
summary: Following Bartolomeu Dias, who had rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488, Vasco da Gama left Lisbon on 8 July 1497 with four ships, sailed around southern Africa and, with a pilot hired at Malindi on the Swahili coast, crossed the Indian Ocean on the monsoon winds. He landed near Calicut in May 1498, but talks with its ruler, the Zamorin, went badly, and only about 55 of his men survived the voyage home in 1499.
why: It opened the first sea route from Europe to Asia, breaking Venice's hold on the spice trade and launching Portugal's maritime empire in the Indian Ocean; with Columbus's voyages it marks the start of the Age of Exploration.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Portuguese discovery of the sea route to India
